title: Home blood-glucose meter
description: Lets people with diabetes check their own blood sugar several times a day and adjust their insulin. A pricked finger puts a drop of blood on a strip whose pad holds an enzyme that reacts with sugar and darkens a dye; the meter shines a light on the pad and reads how much comes back, darker meaning more sugar.
draw: A hand-held meter with a small digital screen, a test strip pushed into its slot; a fingertip with a bead of blood touches the pad at the strip's free end, and a light inside the meter shines on the underside of the coloured pad.
flag: Ames's Glucometer (Elkhart, Indiana) went on sale for home use in November 1981; Ames's Dextrometer (1980) and Boehringer Mannheim's Accu-Chek (Germany) were near-simultaneous. Ames's Reflectance Meter (Anton Clemens, 1970) was for doctors' offices. Today's meters measure a tiny electric current instead of a colour. Overlaps Rapid test strip and Continuous glucose monitor.

title: Geographic information system
description: Lets planners, utilities, farmers and armies ask questions of maps by computer, such as which homes lie on flood-prone ground near a river. Each kind of information, from roads and soils to pipes and land use, is stored as its own layer pinned to the same map coordinates, so the computer can overlay them and pick out where conditions coincide.
draw: A stack of transparent map sheets floating one above another, perfectly aligned over the same patch of land: the bottom one coloured by soil type, then one with a winding river, then one with roads, then one with house outlines; a few houses on the top layer glow where they sit above the river's flood zone.
flag: Changed from 1982: Tomlinson's Canada Geographic Information System, built 1963-68 for the Canada Land Inventory, was the first working GIS (IEEE Milestone 'First GIS, 1962-1968'). 1982 is Esri's ARC/INFO, the first widely sold GIS package; restore it if the card means GIS as a commercial product.

title: Computer-generated imagery
description: Puts on screen things that were never in front of a camera, from film monsters to whole animated films. Every object is built as a mesh of tiny flat triangles; for each dot of the picture the computer works out how light from the lamps bounces off those surfaces into the camera, giving colour, shine and shadow, 24 pictures for every second of film.
draw: A teapot sitting on a chequered floor under a single lamp, its left half drawn as a bare wire mesh of small triangles and its right half smoothly rendered, glossy, with a bright highlight on its belly and a soft shadow falling on the floor away from the lamp.
flag: Collective. 1982 is Tron (MAGI, Triple-I and others) and Star Trek II's Genesis sequence (Lucasfilm), the first big feature-film uses. Earlier: flat computer images in Westworld (1973), a 3D hand and face in Futureworld (1976). First all-computer feature film: Toy Story (1995).

title: Local area network
inventor: Robert Metcalfe and David Boggs, Xerox PARC
description: Wires the computers in an office or home together so they can share files, printers and the internet. Each machine sends data in short packets over a shared cable, listening first; if two start at the same moment, they hear the clash, both stop, and each waits a random instant before trying again. Today a switch usually gives each its own cable.
draw: An office wall with one thick cable running along it at desk height; several desktop computers sit below, each joined to it by a thin drop cable clamped on with a small box, and a bright pulse of light travels along the thick cable from one computer toward the others.
flag: Title dropped '(Ethernet)': brackets are for acronyms, and Ethernet began as a Xerox trademark. Year changed from 1983 to 1973: Metcalfe and Boggs had it running at Xerox PARC by November 1973, linking Alto computers and laser printers (the GUI card is likewise dated by internal Xerox use). First published 1976, DEC-Intel-Xerox standard 1980, first products 1981, IEEE standard 1983.

title: Desktop publishing
description: Lets one person with a computer lay out a newsletter, magazine or book that prints looking professionally typeset. Text and pictures are arranged on an on-screen page that matches the printed one; the page goes to a laser printer as a description of shapes, so each letter is drawn from its outline at the printer's full sharpness.
draw: A beige 1980s desktop computer with a separate square monitor showing a two-column newsletter page, its text as grey lines and one picture box; beside it a desktop laser printer feeding out the same page, the printed sheet half emerged.
flag: 1985 brought together Apple's LaserWriter printer, Adobe's PostScript page language and Aldus PageMaker; Aldus's Paul Brainerd coined the term.

title: Rolling suitcase
description: Lets travellers pull their luggage instead of carrying it. Two small wheels are set into the bottom corners of an upright case, and a handle slides up out of the top on telescoping tubes; tipping the case back onto its wheels puts most of its weight over the axle, so the hand only steadies it and pulls.
draw: Side view of a traveller walking away from the viewer through an airport hall, an upright suitcase trailing behind them and leaning toward them, resting only on the two small wheels at the bottom edge of its face nearest them; the long metal handle rises out of the top of that same face to their hand.
flag: Plath, a Northwest Airlines pilot, built the two-wheeled, telescoping-handle case in 1987 and sold it to aircrews, then the public (Travelpro). Bernard Sadow patented a four-wheeled suitcase pulled flat by a strap in 1970.

title: Direct-to-home satellite TV
description: Brings hundreds of TV channels to any home with a clear view of the sky. A satellite 36,000 km above the equator circles once a day, so it hangs over one spot and beams down microwaves; a small dish focuses them onto a receiver head, which amplifies the faint signal and lowers its frequency so it can run down a cable to the TV.
draw: A small satellite dish fixed to the wall of a house: an oval dish facing up toward the sky at a slant, with a short arm sticking out from its lower edge holding a small receiver head that points back at the middle of the dish, and a cable running from the head down the wall.
flag: 1989 is Sky's launch on SES's Astra 1A satellite, the first mass-market small-dish service (Europe). Japan's NHK broadcast to small dishes from 1984, and big-dish home reception was common in the rural US from about 1980. Overlaps Communications satellites.

title: Motion-sensor chip (MEMS)
description: The accelerometer shrunk onto a silicon chip, cheap enough to fire airbags and turn phone screens. Etching carves a tiny weight hung on silicon springs, with comb-like fingers interleaved with fixed ones; when the chip speeds up or tilts, the weight lags, the gaps between the fingers change, and the chip senses the change in stored electric charge.
draw: A greatly magnified view inside a chip: a flat silicon plate suspended above the base on thin zigzag springs anchored at its corners, with rows of comb fingers sticking out of its sides that slot, without touching, between rows of fixed fingers; the plate is shifted slightly to one side, narrowing the gaps on that side.
flag: Title changed from 'MEMS motion sensors' to put a plain name first. Analog Devices announced its airbag accelerometer chip (ADXL50) in 1991, in volume production 1993. Silicon accelerometers were made in labs from 1979 (Stanford). Gyroscope chips, which sense turning with a vibrating mass, followed in the late 1990s.

title: Contactless card
description: Pays a fare or a bill with a tap, with no battery in the card. A coil of wire loops around the card's edge; the reader's coil makes a rapidly changing magnetic field that induces a current in it, powering the chip, which answers by switching its coil's load on and off, a flicker the reader detects.
draw: A see-through view of a plastic card held flat a few centimetres in front of a reader on a bus: a flat coil of wire looping several times around inside the card's edge, its two ends joined to a tiny chip, and a matching coil visible behind the reader's face.
flag: Changed from 1995: Seoul's bus card was trialled October-December 1995 and opened as a paid service in June 1996, the first contactless card in everyday use, built on Mikron's Mifare chip (Austria, 1994). Hong Kong's Octopus followed in 1997. Location is where it was first used.

title: Home broadband
description: Gives homes an always-on internet connection tens of times faster than dialling up, over wires already there. A cable-TV line carries data in a few spare TV channels. A phone line, built for voice, is split into hundreds of narrow frequency bands above the pitch of speech, each carrying as much data as its noise allows, while calls go on underneath.
draw: A phone socket on a living-room wall with a small splitter plugged in, one lead going to a corded telephone and the other to a small modem box whose lights glow; a cable runs from the modem to an open laptop on a table.
flag: Title shortened from 'Home broadband (DSL and cable modem)'. Year changed from 1997 to 1995: cable internet came first (Jones Intercable, Alexandria, Virginia, October 1995; Rogers, Newmarket, Ontario, November 1995); the first commercial phone-line (ADSL) service was GTE's in California, November 1997. Collective: Rouzbeh Yassini (cable modems), Joseph Lechleider and John Cioffi (DSL).

title: Kinase-inhibitor cancer drugs
description: Pills that hold some cancers in check for years, first of all a leukaemia that used to be fatal. Some cancers are driven by one faulty enzyme, a kinase stuck 'on', that keeps telling cells to divide. The drug is a small molecule shaped to fit the pocket where that kinase takes in its fuel, plugging it so the signal stops.
draw: A folded protein drawn as a twisting ribbon with a deep cleft in one side, and a small drug molecule, shown as linked balls, sitting snugly in the cleft, filling it.
flag: Imatinib (Gleevec), US approval May 2001, for chronic myeloid leukaemia. Made at Ciba-Geigy (now Novartis, Basel) in the early 1990s and taken to patients by Brian Druker in Oregon.

title: Electronic cigarette
description: Delivers nicotine in a mist instead of smoke, with nothing burning. A battery heats a small wire coil wound around a wick soaked in liquid: propylene glycol, glycerine, flavouring and nicotine. The liquid flash-boils off the hot wick, and the vapour cools in the air being sucked through into tiny droplets that the user breathes in.
draw: Cutaway of a pen-shaped device: a battery in the lower half; above it a small clear tank of liquid; a cotton wick passing through holes in the tank wall with a coil of thin wire wound around its middle; an air hole just below the coil and a channel from the coil up to the mouthpiece, with a wisp of mist rising.
flag: Hon Lik, a Beijing pharmacist, invented it in 2003 and it went on sale in China in 2004. His first design made the mist with a vibrating ultrasonic element; the heated coil soon replaced it. Herbert Gilbert patented a smokeless cigarette in 1963 that was never sold.

title: Online maps and navigation
description: Shows any street on Earth, finds the way there and talks you through each turn. The world's maps and satellite photos are cut into square tiles at many zoom levels, so a phone fetches only the few it needs; satellite positioning places you on them, and distant computers plan the route using speed reports from millions of other phones to avoid traffic jams.
draw: A smartphone in a holder on a car dashboard, its screen showing a street map with one route drawn as a thick coloured line and an arrow marking the car's position at a junction; the same junction is visible through the windscreen ahead.
flag: February 2005 is Google Maps, built from the Rasmussen brothers' Where 2 Technologies in Sydney, with satellite photos from Keyhole (US). MapQuest gave web maps and driving directions from 1996; turn-by-turn phone navigation with live traffic came in 2009.

title: OLED display
inventor: Ching Tang and Steven Van Slyke, Kodak
description: The screen in most smartphones and many TVs, thin enough to bend, where each dot makes its own light. Every pixel is a sandwich of thin films of carbon-based molecules between two electrodes; current pushed through makes them glow red, green or blue, and a tiny transistor behind each one sets its brightness. With no backlight, black pixels are simply off.
draw: A thin screen panel bent in a gentle curve, one corner cut away to show its layers: a plastic base, a layer of tiny transistors, a thin glowing layer between two electrode films, and a clear cover on top; the front shows tiny red, green and blue dots glowing.
flag: Tang and Van Slyke made the first efficient OLED at Kodak in 1987. 2007 marks the first OLED TV (Sony, Japan) and mass production of phone screens (Samsung, South Korea); small OLED screens were sold from 1997 (Pioneer car radio) and on a Kodak camera in 2003.

title: Emoji
description: Little pictures typed into messages, so a smile, a heart or a thumbs-up travels with the words. Each emoji is stored as a number code, just like a letter, so any phone can send it; the receiving phone looks the code up in its own font and draws its own picture, which is why the same emoji looks slightly different on different phones.
draw: A hand holding a smartphone showing a chat of message bubbles that contain small round yellow smiling faces, a red heart and a thumbs-up, with the on-screen keyboard open below showing a grid of such little pictures; no readable text.
flag: Changed from 2010: Kurita's set for NTT Docomo's mobile internet (1999) was used by millions in Japan; J-Phone put 90 emoji on one phone in 1997. 2010 is when Unicode added them, taking them worldwide; restore 2010 if that is the event wanted.

title: Rocket interceptor system
description: Shoots down rockets fired at towns, while ignoring those headed for empty ground. A radar tracks each rocket moments after launch and a computer predicts where it will land; only if that is a populated area does it fire an interceptor missile, steered by radio updates and then its own radar to explode beside the rocket in mid-air.
draw: A ground launcher, a box of twenty tubes tilted steeply upward, with one interceptor missile just leaving a tube on a white smoke trail; high in the sky its trail curves to meet a small incoming rocket at a bright burst.
flag: Iron Dome; first interception 7 April 2011, near Ashkelon. Older missile defence (Patriot, from the 1980s) was built against larger missiles and is far too costly per shot for cheap rockets.

title: Software containers
description: Packs a program with everything it needs, so it runs the same on a laptop as on a thousand servers. The operating system walls each container off, giving it its own view of files and network and a fixed share of memory and processor, while all of them share one system underneath, so they start in a second and pack many to a machine.
draw: A rack-mounted server pulled out of its cabinet with its lid off, its circuit board covered by a neat row of small identical sealed boxes like miniature shipping containers, each a different colour, all sitting on the same board and drawing on the same shared bank of memory chips.
flag: Docker, 2013 (dotCloud, San Francisco; Hykes is French). The Linux features it uses came largely from Google (cgroups, 2007), which ran its own services in containers before that; FreeBSD jails (2000) and Solaris Zones (2004) were earlier. Overlaps Cloud data centre; the metaphor echoes Container shipping.

title: Smartwatch
description: A wristwatch that counts steps, tracks sleep, measures the heartbeat and shows messages from the phone. A tiny accelerometer chip feels every step and movement; on the back, green lights shine into the wrist and a light sensor picks up the faint pulsing as blood, which soaks up green light, surges through the vessels with each heartbeat.
draw: A smartwatch on a wrist, shown in cutaway: on the underside of the watch two small green lights glow into the skin beside a dark light sensor, and beneath the skin a blood vessel swells with a pulse; the watch face on top shows a small heart shape.
flag: Title shortened from 'Smartwatch and fitness tracker' (two devices; today's smartwatch does both). Collective. 2015 is the Apple Watch, which with wrist heart-rate bands (Fitbit Charge HR, 2015) made them mass-market; Fitbit's clip-on step counter was 2009 and the Pebble smartwatch 2013.

title: Facial recognition
description: Recognises a person from their face, to unlock a phone, check a passport or pick someone out of a crowd. A neural network trained on millions of photos turns each face into a list of numbers, a point in a space where pictures of the same person land close together; the system checks how close a new face is to stored ones.
draw: A person in a dim room holding a phone up in front of their face, a fine grid of faint red dots projected from the top edge of the phone and curving over their nose, cheeks and forehead to show the face's shape.
flag: Collective. 2017 is phone face unlock with a 3D infrared dot projector (Apple's iPhone X); learned face 'embeddings' came from Facebook (DeepFace, 2014) and Google (FaceNet, 2015). Face matching was used by police and casinos from the late 1990s, and Woody Bledsoe's experiments date from the 1960s.

title: Defibrillator
description: Shocks a quivering heart back into a steady beat. When the heart's muscle fibres twitch out of step it pumps no blood; a capacitor charged to a few thousand volts dumps its charge through two pads on the chest in an instant, stopping every fibre at once so the heart's natural rhythm-setter can restart them together.
draw: A portable defibrillator box open on the floor beside a person lying on their back, two flat adhesive pads stuck on the bare chest, one just below the right collarbone and one on the left side below the armpit, wires running from both pads to the box, and a kneeling rescuer's hands held clear of the body.
flag: Year changed from 1979, which is the first automated external defibrillator (the kind that reads the rhythm itself and tells a bystander when to shock). Beck first saved a patient in 1947 (Cleveland) with paddles on the bare heart during surgery; Paul Zoll shocked through the closed chest in 1956, and Bernard Lown's 1962 capacitor design is the basis of today's machines. The board already has Pacemaker (1957).

title: ACE inhibitors
inventor: Miguel Ondetti and David Cushman, Squibb
description: Pills that lower blood pressure and ease the strain on a failing heart. The body makes a hormone that squeezes blood vessels narrow, and an enzyme snips it into its active form. The drug, modelled on a peptide from a Brazilian snake's venom, plugs that enzyme, so the vessels relax and blood flows at lower pressure.
draw: A cutaway of a small artery drawn twice side by side: on the left its muscular wall clenched tight around a narrow channel, on the right the same artery relaxed and wide with red blood cells flowing freely through it.
flag: Captopril, approved in the US in 1981; it was designed from a venom peptide that Sérgio Ferreira found in a Brazilian pit viper.

title: Recombinant protein drugs
description: Human hormones and proteins made in bulk by microbes, starting with insulin for diabetes, which until then came from pig and cow pancreases. The human gene is spliced into bacteria or yeast, which read it as one of their own and make the human protein; huge fermentation tanks grow them, and the protein is filtered out and purified.
draw: A tall stainless-steel fermentation tank in a factory, cut away to show a frothy broth inside stirred by a central shaft with paddle blades, air bubbling up from a ring at the bottom, pipes and gauges on the outside.
flag: Human insulin, approved in the US in October 1982; Genentech engineered the bacteria (1978) and Lilly made the drug. Overlaps the board's Recombinant DNA (1970) and Genetic engineering (1973) cards.

title: Word processor
description: Lets people type, correct and rearrange writing on a screen before anything is printed. The words sit in the computer's memory as a long string of character codes; inserting or deleting a letter just shifts the rest along, and the program re-flows the lines to fit the page, so a document can be revised endlessly and printed clean.
draw: A late-1970s personal computer with a boxy monitor showing lines of glowing green text with a blinking block cursor in the middle of a line, and beside it a printer with a sheet of neatly typed paper feeding out.
flag: Year changed from 1983 and title shortened from 'Word processor software'. Shrayer's Electric Pencil (December 1976) was the first for personal computers; Wang's screen-based office word processors also arrived in 1976; WordStar (1978) was the first big seller. IBM's magnetic-tape typewriter (1964) was an earlier word processor with no screen.

title: Active-matrix LCD
description: The flat colour screen of laptops, televisions and phones. Each dot of the picture is a tiny window of liquid crystal between polarising filters, which twists light more or less to let it through. Printed on the glass behind each dot is its own transistor switch, which holds the voltage steady between refreshes, so a big screen stays sharp, fast and bright.
draw: A flat screen with one corner peeled apart into its layers: a white backlight at the bottom, a glass sheet with a fine grid of wires and a tiny transistor at the corner of each square cell, a thin liquid-crystal layer, and a top glass sheet with red, green and blue filter stripes.
flag: Brody (Westinghouse, US) built the first active-matrix LCD in 1972-73; Spear and LeComber (Dundee, Scotland) showed in 1979 that amorphous-silicon transistors could be laid on glass; the first product was Seiko Epson's pocket colour TV, Japan, 1984.

title: Conjugate vaccines
inventor: John Robbins and Rachel Schneerson, US National Institutes of Health
description: Protects babies from meningitis and pneumonia caused by bacteria with a sugary coat. Young children's immune systems ignore sugars, so a vaccine of the coat alone fails them; chemically bolting the sugar onto a harmless protein brings the immune system's helper cells in, and the child makes lasting antibodies against the coat.
draw: A molecular-scale view of a single bacterium wrapped in a fuzzy layer of branching sugar chains; beside it, a vaccine particle: a compact, folded protein with several short sugar chains chemically attached to its surface like tassels.
flag: 1987: the first Hib conjugate vaccine licensed in the US (for toddlers; for infants from 1990). Porter Anderson and David Smith (Rochester) developed another version in parallel. Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine followed in 2000.

title: Fly-by-wire airliner
description: An airliner whose controls are worked by computers instead of cables and pulleys. The pilot's small side-stick sends electrical signals to computers, which also read gyroscopes and accelerometers; they then drive hydraulic rams that move the wing and tail surfaces, and refuse any command that would stall the plane or overstress it.
draw: The left side of an airliner cockpit: the captain's hand on a small joystick mounted on the side console beside the window, no control column in front of the seat, and screens across the panel ahead; sky through the windscreen.
flag: Airbus A320, in service April 1988. Concorde (flew 1969, in service 1976) had analogue fly-by-wire with a mechanical backup, and military jets had it in the 1970s; the A320 was the first airliner with digital computers and built-in flight-envelope protection. Uses the board's Accelerometer card.

title: Open-source operating system
description: Free software that runs most of the world's servers, supercomputers and phones, written by thousands of volunteers and companies. Its source code, the human-readable instructions, is published for anyone to read, change and share; changes are sent in over the Internet, reviewed, and merged by maintainers into the next version, which anyone can download.
draw: A plain beige 1990s desktop computer and monitor on a student's desk, the screen showing a black background filled with lines of light-grey start-up text, a stack of floppy disks beside the keyboard.
flag: Linux, announced by Torvalds, a Helsinki student, in August 1991, and combined with the GNU tools that Stallman's project had been writing in the US since 1983. Free BSD Unix versions followed in 1992-93.

title: Secure web connection (SSL/TLS)
description: Keeps passwords and card numbers secret on their way between your browser and a website, and proves the site is genuine. The site presents a certificate vouched for by a trusted authority; the browser uses public-key encryption to agree a fresh secret key with the site, then scrambles everything sent both ways with that key.
draw: A laptop screen showing a web payment form of empty boxes, with a small closed padlock symbol at the left end of the address bar at the top; a hand holds a plain payment card in front of the screen.
flag: SSL 2.0 shipped in Netscape's browser in February-March 1995 (version 1.0 was never released); renamed TLS in 1999.

title: Universal serial bus (USB)
description: One plug that connects keyboards, mice, drives and chargers to any computer. When a device is plugged in, the computer asks what it is; the device answers with a description of itself, and the computer loads the right software, no restart needed. Data then travels one bit after another down a pair of twisted wires, while two more wires carry power.
draw: A close-up of a flat rectangular plug being pushed into a matching socket on the side of a laptop, the plug's metal shell cut away to show four flat gold contacts on a plastic tongue inside, the two outer contacts slightly longer than the two inner ones.
flag: USB 1.0, January 1996, from Intel with Compaq, DEC, IBM, Microsoft, NEC and Nortel; it caught on from 1998. Title kept, though the real name is Universal Serial Bus.

title: Electronic voting machine
description: Counts a whole country's votes within hours, with no paper ballots to lose or misread. The voter presses numbered keys for a candidate and sees their name and photo on a small screen before confirming; each vote is stored in sealed memory, and when the polls close the machine prints a tally and its encrypted results are sent on for adding up.
draw: A small grey voting machine on a table behind a cardboard privacy screen, with a telephone-style numeric keypad, a coloured confirm key, and a small screen above showing a candidate's photo; a voter's finger presses one of the keys.
flag: Year changed from 2000 (when every Brazilian election went electronic): Brazil first used its machines in 1996, for about a third of voters. Earlier: the Video Voter in Illinois towns (1975-80) and India's trial at Parur, Kerala (1982), which a court struck down; India went fully electronic in 2004.

title: Online encyclopedia (wiki)
description: A free encyclopedia that anyone with a web browser can read and edit, with millions of articles in hundreds of languages. Every page has an edit button; each change is saved as a new version, so nothing is lost and a bad edit can be undone in one click, while volunteers watch the stream of recent changes and argue out disputes on discussion pages.
draw: A laptop screen showing an encyclopedia-style page split into two columns of the same paragraph side by side, comparing two versions: one line highlighted in pale red on the left and its replacement in pale green on the right, the text drawn as grey lines.
flag: Wikipedia, launched 15 January 2001. The wiki, a website any visitor can edit, was Ward Cunningham's idea (1995).

title: Distributed version control
description: Lets thousands of programmers work on the same code at once without overwriting each other. Every programmer keeps a full copy of the project and its whole history; each saved change is labelled with a fingerprint calculated from its contents, so copies can be compared and swapped over the Internet, and the software merges different people's edits line by line.
draw: A programmer's monitor showing a dark screen with a branching chart: a vertical line of coloured dots, side lines splitting off from it and later merging back in, each dot a saved version.
flag: Git, written by Torvalds in April 2005 for Linux, after the free licence for BitKeeper (2000) was withdrawn; Mercurial appeared the same month. Torvalds was living in the US by then; location could be Finland.

title: Rotavirus vaccine
description: Drops swallowed by babies that protect them from rotavirus, the commonest cause of deadly diarrhoea in young children. The drops hold live but weakened virus, grown in the lab until it barely makes anyone ill; it multiplies a little in the baby's gut and trains the immune system to fight off the real thing.
draw: A health worker squeezing liquid drops from a small plastic tube into the open mouth of a baby held on its mother's lap.
flag: Year changed from 2006: the lasting vaccine (Rotarix, from Ward and Bernstein's Cincinnati strain, made by GSK) was first licensed in Mexico in July 2004; it reached Europe, and Merck's RotaTeq (Offit, Clark and Plotkin) the US, in 2006. An earlier vaccine, RotaShield (1998), was withdrawn in 1999 after rare bowel blockages.

title: Off-grid solar lighting
inventor: Sam Goldman and Ned Tozun, d.light
description: Gives homes without electricity clean, bright light in place of smoky kerosene lamps. A small solar panel charges a lithium-ion battery during the day; at night the battery powers a white LED, which turns electricity into light so efficiently that a few hours of sunshine runs the lamp all evening, and often charges a phone too.
draw: A child doing homework at night by the light of a small plastic lantern on the table, its white LED shining down; a thin cable runs from the lantern to a small flat solar panel leaning against the wall by the window.
flag: d.light's first lanterns went on sale in 2008, in India and then Africa; the company grew out of a Stanford course (2006-07), so location could be India. Solar lanterns existed from the 1980s but cost too much until cheap white LEDs; pay-as-you-go home solar kits followed in 2011-12 (M-KOPA, Kenya).

title: Biometric digital ID
inventor: Unique Identification Authority of India, Nandan Nilekani
description: Gives each person a number they can prove is theirs with a fingertip or an eye, even with no papers. At enrolment ten fingerprints, both irises and the face are recorded and checked against everyone on file, so nobody gets two numbers; later a scanner at a bank or shop sends a fingerprint to the central computers, which answer yes or no.
draw: A woman pressing her fingertip onto the small glass window of a hand-held fingerprint scanner held out across a shop counter, the scanner wired to a phone, the ridges of her fingertip visible where it presses on the glass.
flag: India's Aadhaar issued its first numbers in September 2010 and now covers over 1.3 billion people. Overlaps Facial recognition (parallel batch); biometric passports (2006) were left out of the list.

title: Ride-hailing apps
description: Summons a car to wherever you are standing with a tap on a phone. The phone sends its satellite-positioning fix to the company's computers, which track every nearby driver on a live map, pick the closest free one, set the fare from distance and demand, and charge your card when the ride ends. Most drivers are ordinary people in their own cars.
draw: A hand holding a smartphone showing a street map with a small car symbol moving along a road toward a pin, while in the background a car pulls up at the kerb of a city street at dusk.
flag: Year changed from 2012: Uber (then UberCab) opened in San Francisco in 2010 with hired black cars; 2012 is when Lyft and UberX let ordinary drivers use their own cars, and China's Didi started. Phone apps for booking taxis date from about 2008.

title: Stroke clot retrieval
description: Pulls the blood clot out of a blocked brain artery during a stroke, often sparing the patient lasting disability. Guided by X-ray, a doctor threads a thin tube from the groin up into the brain and pushes a folded wire-mesh tube through the clot; the mesh springs open, the clot gets caught in it, and both are drawn back out.
draw: A cutaway of a brain artery blocked by a dark red clot; a thin catheter reaches the clot from below, and a cylindrical tube of open metal mesh has expanded inside the clot, the clot's material bulging through the mesh, as it is pulled back toward the catheter.
flag: Kept 2015: five trials that year (MR CLEAN, Netherlands, the first, published in early 2015) proved it works, and it became standard care. The first clot retriever (Merci, a corkscrew wire by Y. Pierre Gobin, UCLA) was approved in the US in 2004; mesh 'stent retrievers' came into use in Europe around 2009 and the US in 2012. Inventor left blank as collective.

title: Grid battery storage
description: Steadies the electricity grid and stores cheap solar and wind power for later. Thousands of lithium-ion cells fill rows of container-sized cabinets, and inverters turn their direct current into the grid's alternating current. When a power station trips and the grid's frequency starts to sag, they push out power within a fraction of a second, far faster than any spinning generator.
draw: Rows of identical white container-sized metal cabinets standing on gravel in open country, cooling fans on their sides, cables running to a small substation with transformers and power lines, a wind turbine in the distance.
flag: Year changed from 2017 (Hornsdale, South Australia, 100 MW, the first very large one): AES and A123's 12 MW lithium-ion plant at Los Andes, Chile, began work in November 2009 doing the same fast-frequency job. Lead-acid batteries did it earlier in West Berlin (from 1986-87), and battery banks backed up city DC networks from the 1890s. Keep 2017 if the card means the big-battery era.

title: FPV attack drone
description: A cheap racing drone turned into a guided bomb. The pilot wears video goggles showing the live view from a small camera in the drone's nose, as if sitting aboard, and steers it by radio straight into a tank, trench or vehicle, where an explosive charge strapped under it goes off. Each costs a few hundred dollars.
draw: A soldier crouching in a trench wearing boxy video goggles and holding a two-stick radio controller, while just above him a small four-propeller drone flies off with a cylindrical explosive charge strapped beneath its frame and a tiny camera pointing forward from its front.
flag: Ukrainian volunteers first adapted hobby racing drones for attack in spring 2022; mass use came in 2023. 'FPV' (first-person view) is a hobbyists' acronym; 'Drone bomb' or 'Kamikaze racing drone' would be plainer titles. Inventor left blank as collective. Overlaps Quadcopter drone (2010) and Military drone (1995).
